## PDF page 122

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=122)

```text
                              RAISING


Calculating the BE% when betting is straight-forward, but we also need to
know what our BE% is when raising.

Each page contains two exercises where you are given the pot size before
you raise and five possible raise sizes. Complete the table below, jotting down
what percentage of the pot each of the raise sizes represents, and the BE%
for each.

Remember that you can use the “3x + original pot” rule to figure out what a
pot-sized raise would be. Raises are more complex since pot-sized raises are
dependent upon the size of your opponent’s original bet.

Pay attention to how BE% relates to the size of your raise compared to the pot.
And when doing these calculations, consider if your opponents would likely
fold more often than the BE% of your raise requires. If yes, are you actively
bluffing this spot in your games?

GLGL.




                                    PA G E 1 2 2
```

## PDF page 125

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=125)

```text
                                  CHAPTER NINE



                          AUTO-PROFIT


A play is auto-profitable when your opponent folds more often than the
breakeven percentage (BE%).

                AU T O -PROF I T = T H E I R FOL D % > B R E A K E V E N %


If you bluff for $600 into $600, your BE% comes out to 50%. If you assume your
opponent would fold 75% of the time against your $600 bet, then the bluff
nets you an auto-profit. Simple.

Auto-profit opportunities are everywhere and they are the focal point for
aggressive players. By comparing the BE% to an estimation of how often your
opponent will fold to a bluff, you can find extra +EV plays in each session.

This is not to say that we can only bluff if it is auto-profitable since there are
other factors at play as well. Rather, by diligently looking for auto-profit spots
we can find ways to increase our bluffing frequency in a way that is backed
by math.

These exercises will help you start tying together concepts like BE% and how
often your opponent will fold given basic assumptions.

TOOLS TO USE: Flopzilla and my “Breakeven Percentage” spreadsheet
available at www.splitsuit.pro/sheets



                                       PA G E 1 2 5
```

## PDF page 126

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=126)

```text
                     P O K E R M AT H & P R E F L O P WO R K B O O K


PROCESS: Plug the range and flop into Flopzilla. Then, based upon the
information in the question, add a filter for the hand categories that would
continue against a bet. Flopzilla then tells you how often your opponent has a
hand that would continue, and if you subtract that percentage from 100% you
see how often your opponent would fold against your bet. Plug that number
into the all five rows in the “Actual Fold-%” column.




Now fill out the rest of the table for each of the five bet sizes. Remember, a
bluff is auto-profitable if your opponent’s actual fold-% is higher than the
breakeven percentage.

TAKEAWAYS: This exercise is simplified since you are not factoring in the
blocking effect of your own hole cards nor how your opponent’s folding fre-
quency might be influenced by different sizes. That said, notice how many
of your bluffs are auto-profitable when the bet sizes are smaller and your
opponent’s continuance range veers toward nutted hands.

GLGL.




                                      PA G E 1 2 6
```
